solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

R067-01.notes: B restates the closing claim (comfort a poor guide; methods that feel least effective sometimes last). A: passage never compares nonsense syllables with real words. C: contradicted by P5 'None of this means that rereading is useless.' D: passage is about method, not amount of study; P1 forgetting curve is not attributed to insufficient study.

R067-02.notes: P1: syllables 'chosen so that no meaning or association could help him.' A: speed of memorizing not mentioned (and the aim was the opposite of making it easier). B: replication not mentioned. D: list length not mentioned.

flags.note: Stem asks which 'result' would have misled the researcher, but the choices are conclusions (A is the mistaken conclusion the five-minute result would support). Consider 'which conclusion would a researcher who tested students only five minutes after studying most likely have drawn mistakenly?' Key is still clear.

R067-03.notes: At five minutes rereaders remembered slightly more, so a five-minute-only test would suggest rereading beats recall, the reverse of the one-week finding. B: the one-week finding, which such a researcher would never see. C: Ebbinghaus's finding, not this experiment, and not visible at five minutes. D: reverses P3; rereaders were more confident.

R067-04.notes: P3: rereaders were more confident but (per P2) remembered less after a week. A: Ebbinghaus is P1. B: no banning argument, and P5 says rereading isn't useless. C: P3 has no new experiment; it reports another result (predictions) from the same study and doesn't contradict it.

R067-05.notes: P4 defines it right away: material 'is processed easily, and that ease feels like mastery.' A/B: common senses of fluency (language, reading aloud) that don't fit the context. D: the illusion is that fluency is mistaken for accurate memory, so fluency itself can't mean accurate memory.

R067-06.notes: The example illustrates 'Effort that leads nowhere... does little good,' qualifying 'not every struggle is productive.' B: the example is offered as unhelpful, the opposite of a recommendation. C: overstates; nothing says rereading beats recall 'in every case.' D: not linked to Ebbinghaus.

R067-07.notes: P1: relearned lists 'stayed with him far longer than lists he crammed in a single sitting.' A: reverses it. C: no comparison with real words. D: 'perfectly' is unsupported.

R067-08.notes: P4: a struggling student 'may conclude that the method is not working, even as the struggle is strengthening the memory.' A: the very mistake the passage warns against. B: overstates; struggle strengthens memory but doesn't prove full learning. C: contradicts P2, where recall's advantage showed up at one week.

R067-09.notes: P5: comfort 'may be a poor guide to what those habits accomplish.' The hedged wording ('may,' 'sometimes') fits 'cautious.' B: reverses the author's view. C: 'never' is too extreme and not 'dismissive' in tone. D: the passage does discuss study habits.

R067-10.notes: P1 Ebbinghaus (early study); P2-3 modern experiment; P4 explanation (illusion of fluency); P5 qualification ('None of this means...'). A: no theory is rejected. B: Ebbinghaus's work isn't a personal story, and there is no list of tips. D: no solution is shown to fail.
